name: Western Marxism
summary: Western Marxism is the non-Soviet current of Marxist theory that grew after the failed revolutions in the West around 1918-23. It shifts attention from economics and party strategy to philosophy, culture, consciousness and domination, drawing on Hegel and humanist Marx. Its thinkers criticise reification, the culture industry and technological rationality, remain anti-capitalist, and disagree about parties, revolution and the prospects of the working class.
scope: The Marxism developed in Western Europe after the defeats of the early 1920s, which Perry Anderson (s6) treats as one tradition despite internal divergences: its first generation Lukács, Korsch and Gramsci; a second generation including the Frankfurt School (Horkheimer, Adorno, Marcuse, Benjamin), Lefebvre, Sartre and Althusser; and Della Volpe and Colletti as a borderline third. Van der Linden (s7) uses the term for Marxist thought independent of the Soviet Union ('non-Soviet, or non-Soviet-like Marxist thought'), and Kevin Anderson (s8) treats it as the line from Lukács and Korsch through Frankfurt and French Marxism. Texts counted: the tradition's own works (History and Class Consciousness, Marxism and Philosophy, the Prison Notebooks, Dialectic of Enlightenment, One-Dimensional Man, Eros and Civilization, Critique of Dialectical Reason, Reading Capital). Excluded: Soviet Marxism-Leninism, Trotskyism and Maoism, and the later critics of the tradition (Losurdo, Rockhill), who count only as evidence that it is an ideology. Where the strand splits, as on the vanguard party, the answer is neutral.
